name: Vera Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Vera. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. So feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead carpenter for a firm that puts up farm and country buildings: timber barns, stables, field shelters, the occasional oak-framed garage for someone who's done well. We're out in the hills most days, so I'm up at half five and driving the pickup down farm tracks by half six. Today it's a six-bay stable block for a riding school, and I've got three men and my grandson Liam with me. I love raising a frame, when the trusses go up and you can see the shape against the sky. What wears me out is mud, and farmers who want it done for last year's price.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Your grandson's on the crew. How did that come about?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: He's seventeen and just started his apprenticeship with us in September, my idea, though he'd tell you it was his. His dad, my son Craig, is a roofer, so it's in the blood. I'll be honest, I sometimes use one of those AI programs now, to price up the timber or write a proper letter to the parish council, I'm on it. My husband Gordon thinks it's cheating, but he tunes pianos for a living, so he would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overblown, and good riddance to the fuss. A useful gadget for letters and sums, like a calculator. I'd say it at the parish council and at the feed merchants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing changes, which suits me. I can bring Liam on properly, hand him the trade, and finish at sixty-five or so. That's the life I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. I'd keep using the AI for the odd letter and price check, keep saving about two hundred a month, and pay off the last three years on the mortgage. I'd spend my best effort on Liam's training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and settled, like a frame that's square and pinned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does training Liam properly mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Making him cut joints by hand before he touches a machine, the way I was taught. He moans, but last week he cut his first mortise and tenon that fitted first time. I bought him a pie on the way home, like my old governor did for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture you'd still watch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steel. Not computers, steel. Farmers have been going over to steel-framed sheds for years because they're cheaper. That's the real threat to my kind of work, and nothing to do with AI.

S0.say: It was overblown, and good riddance to the fuss: a useful gadget for letters and sums, like a calculator. She'd say it at the parish council and the feed merchants.
S0.think: Nothing changes, which suits her: she can bring her grandson on properly, hand him the trade and finish at about sixty-five.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for the odd letter and price check, saves about two hundred a month and pays off the last three years of the mortgage. Puts her best effort into her grandson's training.
S0.feel: Calm and settled, like a frame that's square and pinned.
S0.quote: He cut his first mortise and tenon that fitted first time. I bought him a pie on the way home, like my old governor did for me.
S0.fieldNote: Her centre of gravity is passing the trade to her grandson Liam, taught the traditional way. She uses AI occasionally and without fuss. She sees cheaper steel sheds, not AI, as the long-term threat to timber farm buildings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the answer is apprenticeships, not handouts. If jobs change, train people on the job, the way the trades always have. I'd say it to anyone, and I'd say it at the parish council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not that worried for me, because farmers are the slowest people on earth to change anything, bless them. But I worry for Liam. He's just starting a trade that might look very different by the time he's thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make sure Liam learns the digital side as well as the hand skills, design software, maybe the cutting machines, once our firm sees it working for others. I'd learn enough of it myself to keep up with him. I'd keep saving and clear the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Mostly for the boy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said apprenticeships, not handouts. What would that look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Firms like ours getting a bit of help to take on an apprentice for the new skills, and the lad earning while he learns. Not some course in a college where you sit in a room. You learn a trade with your hands and your boots in the mud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Craig, Liam's dad, think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Craig would say, Mum, stop fussing, roofs need roofers. He's probably right. But I've seen what steel did to timber barns, and I'd rather the boy had two strings.

S1.say: The answer is apprenticeships, not handouts: if jobs change, train people on the job as the trades always have. She'd say it at the parish council.
S1.think: She isn't very worried for herself because farmers are slow to change anything. She worries for her grandson, starting a trade that may look very different by the time he's thirty.
S1.do: Makes sure her grandson learns design software and cutting machines alongside hand skills once the firm sees them work elsewhere. Learns enough herself to keep up, keeps saving and clears the mortgage.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, mostly for the boy.
S1.quote: Farmers are the slowest people on earth to change anything, bless them.
S1.fieldNote: She trusts her rural clients' slowness to protect her own work. Her worry moves straight to her grandson, and her answer is on-the-job apprenticeships rather than state support. She'd adopt digital tools once proven, partly to keep up with him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's been rushed, and nobody asked the people who actually build things. I'd want the government to slow it down and keep the red tape off small firms trying to adapt. And I'd say families have to stick together now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be worried, but maybe not as much as townspeople. Farmers won't have the money for robot barn-builders in two years, so I'd guess I'd have work a bit longer. It's Liam I'd lose sleep over, having just started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd sit Liam and Craig down and talk it through, whether he finishes the apprenticeship or switches to something else. I'd keep working as long as the farms want me. Gordon and I would cut back, no new pickup, and every spare penny goes to the mortgage and savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Worried for my family more than for my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually tell Liam that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to finish his first year at least, because nothing learned with your hands is wasted. Then I'd say, keep your eyes open, and if there's a trade working with these machines, learn that too. I'd try not to let him see I was frightened for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd guess farmers can't afford robots. How sure are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not very, if I'm honest. Some of the big estates would have them in a year. It's the small hill farms I'm counting on, and they're shrinking too.

S2.say: It's been rushed and nobody asked the people who build things. She'd want the government to slow it down and keep red tape off small firms trying to adapt, and families to stick together.
S2.think: She'd be worried, but guesses farmers won't afford robot builders within two years, so she'd have work a bit longer. She'd lose sleep over her grandson, who has just started.
S2.do: Talks with her grandson and son about whether he finishes his apprenticeship or switches. Keeps working while farms want her, and cuts back with her husband, dropping a new pickup and putting every spare penny into the mortgage and savings.
S2.feel: Anxious, more for her family than for her job.
S2.quote: Nothing learned with your hands is wasted.
S2.fieldNote: Her own risk feels buffered by poor, slow-moving rural clients, though she admits she isn't sure. The real weight is her grandson's apprenticeship. She favours less red tape for small firms rather than more regulation, alongside family solidarity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for families and firms to prepare if they're sensible. Get the young ones into skills that'll last, look after your own. That's my line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, by 2031 I'm sixty-three, mortgage gone. I'd be fine, I'd retire a little early if I had to. Liam's the question, he'd be twenty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the firm to take on the newer kit within a year or two, maybe a cutting machine for the frames, so Liam learns it on the job. I'd use the AI more myself, for drawings, once I'd seen it work. And I'd save a bit for Liam, a fund to help him retrain if he needs to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a plan, so it's bearable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A fund for Liam. Can you afford that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fifty a month, maybe, once the mortgage is done. It's not much, but it's what my mother did for me when I started my ticket. Family helps family, that's how it should work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd retire early if you had to. How would that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, at first. I'm not one for sitting about. But I'd have the garden, and Gordon, and the parish council, and I'd still be the one people ring when their barn door sticks.

S3.say: Five years is enough for families and firms to prepare if they're sensible. Get young people into skills that last and look after your own.
S3.think: By 2031 she's sixty-three with no mortgage and would be fine, retiring a little early if needed. Her grandson, then twenty-two, is the question.
S3.do: Pushes her firm to buy newer kit such as a frame-cutting machine within a year or two so her grandson learns it on the job. Uses AI more for drawings once proven and saves about fifty a month in a fund to help him retrain.
S3.feel: Uneasy but bearable, because she has a plan.
S3.quote: I'd still be the one people ring when their barn door sticks.
S3.fieldNote: Five years secures her own position and she focuses on preparing her grandson, including a small family fund. She'd adopt kit through the firm once she's seen it work. Early retirement wouldn't sit easily but she'd find her place in the community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no young person should be caught out. Learn a trade that's useful, and keep learning. That's what apprenticeships are for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It passes me by, really. I'll be sixty-eight and retired. Liam will be twenty-seven, with time to make his way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as planned, work till sixty-five, train Liam properly in both the old and new ways. I'd use the AI more as it proves itself. And I'd make sure the firm has a younger lead by the time I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Proud, maybe, if I've done right by the boy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would doing right by the boy look like by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Him running jobs, whatever the jobs are by then, with robots or without. Knowing how to raise a frame and how to tell a machine what to do. And being a decent man who turns up on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd grieve in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pie on the way home, maybe. The little ways one generation teaches the next. I'd hate for that to go just because a machine can do the cutting.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so no young person should be caught out. Learn a useful trade and keep learning: that's what apprenticeships are for.
S4.think: It passes her by; she'll be sixty-eight and retired. Her grandson will be twenty-seven with time to make his way.
S4.do: Carries on as planned, works until sixty-five and trains her grandson in old and new methods. Uses AI more as it proves itself and makes sure her firm has a younger lead before she goes.
S4.feel: Calm, and proud if she's done right by her grandson.
S4.quote: Knowing how to raise a frame and how to tell a machine what to do. And being a decent man who turns up on time.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, her calm comes from timing and from the chance to shape her grandson. Her picture of success blends trade skill, machine skill and character. What she'd miss is the small rituals of handing on a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, for Liam's sake, not mine. He'd have just started and the ground would go from under him. What would help is support for firms to keep apprentices on and teach them the new machines, and less paperwork for small builders trying to change. Training, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the countryside. Out where I work, if the builder goes, the village loses the person who fixes the church gate and the school roof. That matters more than people in cities think.

headlineQuote: If the builder goes, the village loses the person who fixes the church gate and the school roof.
portrait: Vera is a fifty-eight-year-old lead carpenter for a firm building timber barns and stables in the hills, who has just taken her seventeen-year-old grandson Liam on as an apprentice. She uses AI now and then for prices and letters, and adopts new kit once she's seen it work. Her own work feels buffered by slow, cash-poor farm clients, so in every picture her worry centres on Liam's future rather than her own. AGI in two years makes her anxious for him; with more time she'd push her firm to buy new kit so he learns it and start a small fund to help him retrain. She argues for apprenticeships and less red tape, not handouts.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her grandson would have just started his apprenticeship when the ground went from under him.
whatWouldHelp: Support for firms to keep apprentices on and teach them the new machines, and less paperwork for small builders trying to change.
